tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

schema.name: ScheduleWakeup
schema.description:

For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. - **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size stays on that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane) until you call this tool again with preset "desktop", so reset it once you are done testing. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent, 5 touch points, and mouse-to-touch translation (hover stops producing hover states). Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.

schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

1	# Skills — What They Are and How to Use Them
2	
3	This is the canonical reference for every skill in this folder. If you're looking for _why_
4	the skill system exists (the human-in-the-lead design philosophy), see the
5	[Human-in-the-Lead AI Development — Project Setup Overview](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305102849)
6	Confluence page (Part 2: AI Governance Layer) —
7	that page covers the rationale; this file covers the _mechanics_: what each skill does, what
8	to pass it, and what it hands back.
9	
10	## How skills work
11	
12	- Invoke a skill by typing `/skill-name` (optionally followed by an argument) in a Claude
13	  Code session. Each skill is a structured, reviewable process defined in its own
14	  `<skill-name>/SKILL.md` file — not a freeform prompt.
15	- Where a skill takes an argument, its `SKILL.md` uses `$ARGUMENTS` to capture whatever
16	  follows the skill name, e.g. `/new-component productBadge` or `/audit-tier overrides/app/hooks/use-wish-list.ts`.
17	  If you invoke a skill with no argument and one is expected, Claude asks for it.
18	- Every skill is **human-in-the-lead**: it either stops for confirmation at a defined
19	  checkpoint, or produces a read-only report/plan rather than making changes outright.
20	  See the checkpoint column in each table below.
21	- These `SKILL.md` files are also the master source for `.cursor/rules/skills/*.mdc` and
22	  `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md` — see [scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs](../../scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs).
23	  Edit the `SKILL.md` here, then run `npm run sync:ai-rules:fix`; never edit the generated
24	  Cursor/VS Code files directly.
25	
26	## Setup & onboarding
27	
28	| Skill                                      | Usage            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                      |
29	| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
30	| [`/session-start`](session-start/SKILL.md) | `/session-start` | Confirms the current branch is safe to work on, reads `.docs/memory/` tracking docs, runs health checks, and states current project position. Run at the **start of every session**.                                                                                                                 | Waits for you to confirm direction before writing any code        |
31	| [`/onboarding`](onboarding/SKILL.md)       | `/onboarding`    | Interactive walkthrough for a new developer or QA engineer — role and squad questions, mechanical setup checks (git hooks, Node version, branch), then role-specific orientation to the rules and tools. Run on a **first session on a new machine or first day on the project**.                    | Confirms understanding at each phase before moving on             |
32	| [`/project-init`](project-init/SKILL.md)   | `/project-init`  | One-time project setup walkthrough — runs `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`, fixes automatable failures, then asks one question at a time for items that need a human answer (Jira prefix, BrowserStack, secrets, Zephyr product, etc.), updating the [7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305430530) Confluence page as it goes. | Asks one question at a time, waits for the answer before the next |
33	
34	## Planning & safety
35	
36	| Skill                                    | Usage                                               | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                             |
37	| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
38	| [`/feature-spec`](feature-spec/SKILL.md) | `/feature-spec <plain-English feature description>` | Turns a feature request into a scoped implementation spec **before any code is written** — clarifies requirements one question at a time, researches the codebase in parallel, checks sprint scope, then outputs a spec with file list, tier flags, and a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. | Produces a plan only — you review the spec before implementation begins  |
39	| [`/scope-check`](scope-check/SKILL.md)   | `/scope-check <a proposed Claude Code prompt>`      | Reviews a prompt _before you run it_ — classifies every file it would likely touch by protection tier, flags drift risk (refactoring upward, cross-squad reach), and verdicts it SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED. Rewrites risky prompts into safely-scoped ones.                                     | You see the blast radius and verdict before the risky prompt is ever run |
40	| [`/audit-tier`](audit-tier/SKILL.md)     | `/audit-tier <file or directory path>`              | Identifies the protection tier (1–4), owner, and import blast radius of a path under `overrides/`. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.                                                                                                                                          | Tells you who to notify before you touch the file                        |
41	
42	## Development
43

# Skills — What They Are and How to Use Them

This is the canonical reference for every skill in this folder. If you're looking for _why_
the skill system exists (the human-in-the-lead design philosophy), see the
[Human-in-the-Lead AI Development — Project Setup Overview](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305102849)
Confluence page (Part 2: AI Governance Layer) —
that page covers the rationale; this file covers the _mechanics_: what each skill does, what
to pass it, and what it hands back.

## How skills work

- Invoke a skill by typing `/skill-name` (optionally followed by an argument) in a Claude
  Code session. Each skill is a structured, reviewable process defined in its own
  `<skill-name>/SKILL.md` file — not a freeform prompt.
- Where a skill takes an argument, its `SKILL.md` uses `$ARGUMENTS` to capture whatever
  follows the skill name, e.g. `/new-component productBadge` or `/audit-tier overrides/app/hooks/use-wish-list.ts`.
  If you invoke a skill with no argument and one is expected, Claude asks for it.
- Every skill is **human-in-the-lead**: it either stops for confirmation at a defined
  checkpoint, or produces a read-only report/plan rather than making changes outright.
  See the checkpoint column in each table below.
- These `SKILL.md` files are also the master source for `.cursor/rules/skills/*.mdc` and
  `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md` — see [scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs](../../scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs).
  Edit the `SKILL.md` here, then run `npm run sync:ai-rules:fix`; never edit the generated
  Cursor/VS Code files directly.

## Setup & onboarding

| Skill                                      | Usage            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                      |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`/session-start`](session-start/SKILL.md) | `/session-start` | Confirms the current branch is safe to work on, reads `.docs/memory/` tracking docs, runs health checks, and states current project position. Run at the **start of every session**.                                                                                                                 | Waits for you to confirm direction before writing any code        |
| [`/onboarding`](onboarding/SKILL.md)       | `/onboarding`    | Interactive walkthrough for a new developer or QA engineer — role and squad questions, mechanical setup checks (git hooks, Node version, branch), then role-specific orientation to the rules and tools. Run on a **first session on a new machine or first day on the project**.                    | Confirms understanding at each phase before moving on             |
| [`/project-init`](project-init/SKILL.md)   | `/project-init`  | One-time project setup walkthrough — runs `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`, fixes automatable failures, then asks one question at a time for items that need a human answer (Jira prefix, BrowserStack, secrets, Zephyr product, etc.), updating the [7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305430530) Confluence page as it goes. | Asks one question at a time, waits for the answer before the next |

## Planning & safety

| Skill                                    | Usage                                               | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`/feature-spec`](feature-spec/SKILL.md) | `/feature-spec <plain-English feature description>` | Turns a feature request into a scoped implementation spec **before any code is written** — clarifies requirements one question at a time, researches the codebase in parallel, checks sprint scope, then outputs a spec with file list, tier flags, and a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. | Produces a plan only — you review the spec before implementation begins  |
| [`/scope-check`](scope-check/SKILL.md)   | `/scope-check <a proposed Claude Code prompt>`      | Reviews a prompt _before you run it_ — classifies every file it would likely touch by protection tier, flags drift risk (refactoring upward, cross-squad reach), and verdicts it SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED. Rewrites risky prompts into safely-scoped ones.                                     | You see the blast radius and verdict before the risky prompt is ever run |
| [`/audit-tier`](audit-tier/SKILL.md)     | `/audit-tier <file or directory path>`              | Identifies the protection tier (1–4), owner, and import blast radius of a path under `overrides/`. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.                                                                                                                                          | Tells you who to notify before you touch the file                        |

## Development

| Skill                                      | Usage                            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                    |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`/new-component`](new-component/SKILL.md) | `/new-component <componentName>` | Scaffolds a new Zimmermann component under `overrides/app/components/` — TypeScript, Chakra-first, folder layout and props typing per `.claude/rules/conventions.md`/`components.md`/`css.md`, paired Storybook story, optional test file. | You name the component and confirm the resulting file structure |

## Quality & review

| Skill                                    | Usage                                                                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`/code-quality`](code-quality/SKILL.md) | `/code-quality [file or directory]` (no argument = files changed on the current branch) | **Read-only** audit against `.claude/rules/conventions.md`, `typescript.md`, `css.md`, and `components.md` — naming/structure, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence. Produces a prioritised 🔴/🟡/🔵 report. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR. | Report only — you decide what to fix and when                                  |
| [`/pr-checklist`](pr-checklist/SKILL.md) | `/pr-checklist`                                                                         | Runs `/code-quality` on the current branch's changed files, classifies each by tier and reviewer requirement, and generates a copy-paste-ready PR description with a test checklist. Pairs with `/code-quality`.                             | You review and submit the generated PR description — nothing is posted for you |

## QA / testing

| Skill                                  | Usage                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                                    |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`/qa-generate`](qa-generate/SKILL.md) | `/qa-generate` (then answers Jira story questions) | Two-step, human-gated E2E test generation: drafts a Gherkin `.feature` file and **stops completely**; only generates the Playwright spec after Lead QA has explicitly validated (and optionally annotated) the feature file. Use for any new storefront user journey needing E2E coverage. | Playwright spec is not generated until Lead QA signs off on the `.feature` file |

## Contentful

| Skill                                                                      | Usage                                                                                                  | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                               | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`/contentful-register-component`](contentful-register-component/SKILL.md) | `/contentful-register-component <component file path>`                                                 | Reads an existing component's TypeScript props, generates a `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file mapping each prop to a Contentful variable type, and wires it into the `defineComponents` registry.            | You review the generated definition (and any skipped/ambiguous props) before it's published in Contentful |
| [`/contentful-drift-check`](contentful-drift-check/SKILL.md)               | `/contentful-drift-check [component or directory path]` (no argument = scan all registered components) | **Read-only** comparison of component props against their paired Contentful definitions — reports added props, removed props, and type mismatches. Use after props change, or to audit everything at once. | Report only — you resolve any drift found                                                                 |

## Release management

| Skill                                                    | Usage                                                                                    | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Human-in-the-lead checkpoint                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`/generate-changelog`](generate-changelog/SKILL.md)     | `/generate-changelog` (then answers version/range questions)                             | Builds a structured, four-audience changelog (dev team, QA, product, GitHub Release) from conventional commits and the upstream baseline. Writes to `docs/releases/`. Use before cutting a release branch.                                      | You review the changelog before it's published; the GitHub Release command is proposed, never run automatically |
| [`/upstream-sync-review`](upstream-sync-review/SKILL.md) | `/upstream-sync-review` (then supply a candidate `@salesforce/retail-react-app` version) | Reviews upstream release notes against `.docs/memory/upstreamBaseline.md`, maps changes to our override surface, and recommends BUMP / DEFER / WAIT — per the "read the changelog, bump opportunistically" policy in `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md`. | Recommendation only — you approve and run the actual `npm install` bump                                         |

## Adding a new skill

1. Create `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` frontmatter (see any existing skill for the format).
2. Add it to the appropriate table above.
3. Add it to the skill list in [scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs](../../scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs) so it gets mirrored to `.cursor/rules/skills/` and `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md`, then run `npm run sync:ai-rules:fix`.
4. If it belongs in the [Project Setup Overview](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305102849) Confluence page's "Part 2" narrative, add a one-line mention there — but keep the detailed reference here to avoid duplication.

description: Identify the protection tier, owner, and import blast radius of a file or directory under overrides/. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.
---

Identify the protection tier and owner of a file or directory in this codebase.

The path to audit is: $ARGUMENTS

## What to output

**1. Tier**
- Tier 1 (Frozen) — must not be modified without explicit owner approval
- Tier 2 (Protected) — feature branch only, requires second-developer PR review
- Tier 3 (Squad-owned) — only the owning squad should be prompting Claude here
- Tier 4 (Feature-local) — freely editable on a feature branch

Check against:
- [.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md](../../rules/frozenFiles.md) for Tier 1
- [.claude/rules/protectedFiles.md](../../rules/protectedFiles.md) for Tier 2
- `.claude/rules/squadA.md` and `.claude/rules/squadB.md` for Tier 3 *(if absent, infer from path: checkout/cart/payments = Squad A; PDP/PLP/search/account = Squad B)*

**2. Owner**
Design System / Integration / SI Partner / Squad A / Squad B / Both Squads

**3. Can Claude Code modify it?**
- Tier 1: No. Developer must name the file explicitly in the prompt AND confirm owner approval.
- Tier 2: Yes on a feature branch — second-developer PR review required before merging.
- Tier 3: Yes — but only the owning squad should be running Claude in this area.
- Tier 4: Yes, freely.

**4. Import blast radius**
Run this to check how many non-test, non-story files import it (from `overrides/app/` — the customisation surface):
```bash

  | grep -v '\.test\.' | grep -v '\.stories\.' | wc -l
```
If more than 5, flag it as **high blast radius** — a change here breaks many consumers.

**5. Next step**
Specific action for the developer — e.g.:
- "Message #design-system before asking Claude to touch this"

1	---
2	name: code-quality
3	description: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
4	---
5	
6	Audit code quality for the specified scope. Do not modify any files — this is a read-only
7	diagnostic. Produce a prioritised report with actionable fixes.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Input
12	
13	The user will provide one of:
14	- A file path or directory to audit
15	- No argument — default to files changed on the current branch: `git diff --name-only main`
16	
17	If no argument is given, run: `git diff --name-only main` and audit those files.
18	Exclude test files (`*.test.ts`, `*.spec.ts`), stories (`*.stories.tsx`), and any registry files.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Parallel execution
23	
24	For audits covering more than 5 files, split into four independent checks and run them
25	as parallel agents simultaneously. Each agent receives only its own checklist — do not
26	bundle all checks into one agent.
27	
28	- **Agent A — Naming & structure**
29	- **Agent B — Import analysis**
30	- **Agent C — TypeScript coverage**
31	- **Agent D — Test & story coverage**
32	
33	For 5 files or fewer, run all checks sequentially in a single pass.
34	
35	---
36	
37	## Agent A — Naming & structure
38	
39	Rules are defined once, split across [.claude/rules/conventions.md](../../rules/conventions.md)
40	(cross-cutting), [css.md](../../rules/css.md) (Chakra/styling), and
41	[components.md](../../rules/components.md) (components/hooks/Storybook) — read the relevant
42	ones first, then apply each rule to the files in scope. Do not re-list the rules here;
43	that's how the files drift apart.
44	
45	Walk the file list and audit each file against the relevant section:
46	
47	- Every file → conventions.md **General** section.
48	- Every file with JSX/Chakra props → css.md **Tokens** section (no hardcoded hex/px values).
49	- `.tsx` under `overrides/app/components/` or `overrides/app/pages/` → components.md
50	  **Components** + **Composition** sections, plus conventions.md **File naming and folder
51	  structure**.
52	- `.ts` under `overrides/app/hooks/` → components.md **Hooks** section.
53	- `.ts` under `overrides/app/utils/` → conventions.md **Utilities** section.
54	
55	For each violation, record `file:line` and which rule file + bullet failed — the section
56	anchor is enough (e.g. "components.md → Components → Props type placement").
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Agent B — Import analysis
61	
62	For each file, read the import statements and check:
63	
64	- No circular imports: if File A imports from File B, File B must not import from File A
65	  (check by reading the imported file's imports in turn — one level deep is sufficient).
66	- No imports from a higher tier without justification:
67	  - A component must not import directly from internal `commerce-sdk-react` source paths.
68	  - A page must not bypass its own hooks to call raw API functions.
69	- No imports from a later-sprint feature (reference `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` when present).
70	- No `../../../..` chains longer than 3 levels — flag for path alias review.
71	
72	---
73	
74	## Agent C — TypeScript coverage
75	
76	Check each file against the relevant rule file:
77	
78	- Every `.ts`/`.tsx` → [typescript.md](../../rules/typescript.md) in full (no `any` without
79	  justification, `type` vs `interface`, non-null assertions, discriminated unions, utility
80	  types, `import type`, `satisfies`, `readonly`, generic naming).
81	- Components → [components.md](../../rules/components.md) **Components** (props type name,
82	  placement, optional `?`, callback naming, JSDoc).
83	- Hooks → [components.md](../../rules/components.md) **Hooks** (typed params, explicit
84	  return type, JSDoc with `@returns`).
85	
86	Then run `npx tsc --noEmit` **once** for the whole branch (not per file) and report any
87	errors. Cross-reference any new errors against the files in scope.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## Agent D — Test & story coverage
92	
93	For each component file under `overrides/app/components/` or `overrides/app/pages/`:
94	- A paired `*.stories.tsx` exists in the same directory (required by [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) > Testing).
95	- For logic-heavy components or hooks: the component's **own** `*.test.ts`/`*.test.tsx` exists
96	  in the same folder. A `play` function elsewhere (this component's own story, or — this is
97	  the common miss — a *different* component's assembly-level story) does not substitute for
98	  it, even when it happens to exercise the same rendered output; see testing.md's note under
99	  "What to test (and what to skip)". A component's own test file may still mock a hook or
100	  child component whose internals are covered elsewhere — the point is that the component's
101	  own render-branch/event-wiring contract has a test discoverable from its own folder.
102	- If a test file exists, verify:
103	  - At least one test covers the primary render case.
104	  - At least one test covers a user interaction (click, input) if the component has interactive elements.
105	  - No tests use `toBeTruthy()` as the sole assertion — check for meaningful assertions.
106	- If a paired `.stories.tsx` is missing, flag as MISSING STORY (mandatory).
107	- If a logic-heavy file has no test file of its own, flag as MISSING TEST — regardless of
108	  whether a `play` function exists somewhere else in the codebase.
109	
110	For each utility file under `overrides/app/utils/`:
111	- **`.test.ts` required** when the utility has ≥1 conditional branch or performs ≥1
112	  transformation (currency, locale, mapping, parsing, etc.). Trivial re-exports and
113	  one-liners are exempt.
114	- If a test file exists, verify it covers both the happy path and at least one edge case
115	  (empty input, null, locale variation — whichever applies).
116	
117	---
118	
119	## Output format
120	
121	Combine all agent results into a single prioritised report:
122	
123	```
124	## Code Quality Report
125	**Scope:** [files audited]

---
name: code-quality
description: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
---

Audit code quality for the specified scope. Do not modify any files — this is a read-only
diagnostic. Produce a prioritised report with actionable fixes.

---

## Input

The user will provide one of:
- A file path or directory to audit
- No argument — default to files changed on the current branch: `git diff --name-only main`

If no argument is given, run: `git diff --name-only main` and audit those files.
Exclude test files (`*.test.ts`, `*.spec.ts`), stories (`*.stories.tsx`), and any registry files.

---

## Parallel execution

For audits covering more than 5 files, split into four independent checks and run them
as parallel agents simultaneously. Each agent receives only its own checklist — do not
bundle all checks into one agent.

- **Agent A — Naming & structure**
- **Agent B — Import analysis**
- **Agent C — TypeScript coverage**
- **Agent D — Test & story coverage**

For 5 files or fewer, run all checks sequentially in a single pass.

---

## Agent A — Naming & structure

Rules are defined once, split across [.claude/rules/conventions.md](../../rules/conventions.md)
(cross-cutting), [css.md](../../rules/css.md) (Chakra/styling), and
[components.md](../../rules/components.md) (components/hooks/Storybook) — read the relevant
ones first, then apply each rule to the files in scope. Do not re-list the rules here;
that's how the files drift apart.

Walk the file list and audit each file against the relevant section:

- Every file → conventions.md **General** section.
- Every file with JSX/Chakra props → css.md **Tokens** section (no hardcoded hex/px values).
- `.tsx` under `overrides/app/components/` or `overrides/app/pages/` → components.md
  **Components** + **Composition** sections, plus conventions.md **File naming and folder
  structure**.
- `.ts` under `overrides/app/hooks/` → components.md **Hooks** section.
- `.ts` under `overrides/app/utils/` → conventions.md **Utilities** section.

For each violation, record `file:line` and which rule file + bullet failed — the section
anchor is enough (e.g. "components.md → Components → Props type placement").

---

## Agent B — Import analysis

For each file, read the import statements and check:

- No circular imports: if File A imports from File B, File B must not import from File A
  (check by reading the imported file's imports in turn — one level deep is sufficient).
- No imports from a higher tier without justification:
  - A component must not import directly from internal `commerce-sdk-react` source paths.
  - A page must not bypass its own hooks to call raw API functions.
- No imports from a later-sprint feature (reference `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` when present).
- No `../../../..` chains longer than 3 levels — flag for path alias review.

---

## Agent C — TypeScript coverage

Check each file against the relevant rule file:

- Every `.ts`/`.tsx` → [typescript.md](../../rules/typescript.md) in full (no `any` without
  justification, `type` vs `interface`, non-null assertions, discriminated unions, utility
  types, `import type`, `satisfies`, `readonly`, generic naming).
- Components → [components.md](../../rules/components.md) **Components** (props type name,
  placement, optional `?`, callback naming, JSDoc).
- Hooks → [components.md](../../rules/components.md) **Hooks** (typed params, explicit
  return type, JSDoc with `@returns`).

Then run `npx tsc --noEmit` **once** for the whole branch (not per file) and report any
errors. Cross-reference any new errors against the files in scope.

---

## Agent D — Test & story coverage

For each component file under `overrides/app/components/` or `overrides/app/pages/`:
- A paired `*.stories.tsx` exists in the same directory (required by [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) > Testing).
- For logic-heavy components or hooks: the component's **own** `*.test.ts`/`*.test.tsx` exists
  in the same folder. A `play` function elsewhere (this component's own story, or — this is
  the common miss — a *different* component's assembly-level story) does not substitute for
  it, even when it happens to exercise the same rendered output; see testing.md's note under
  "What to test (and what to skip)". A component's own test file may still mock a hook or
  child component whose internals are covered elsewhere — the point is that the component's
  own render-branch/event-wiring contract has a test discoverable from its own folder.
- If a test file exists, verify:
  - At least one test covers the primary render case.
  - At least one test covers a user interaction (click, input) if the component has interactive elements.
  - No tests use `toBeTruthy()` as the sole assertion — check for meaningful assertions.
- If a paired `.stories.tsx` is missing, flag as MISSING STORY (mandatory).
- If a logic-heavy file has no test file of its own, flag as MISSING TEST — regardless of
  whether a `play` function exists somewhere else in the codebase.

For each utility file under `overrides/app/utils/`:
- **`.test.ts` required** when the utility has ≥1 conditional branch or performs ≥1
  transformation (currency, locale, mapping, parsing, etc.). Trivial re-exports and
  one-liners are exempt.
- If a test file exists, verify it covers both the happy path and at least one edge case
  (empty input, null, locale variation — whichever applies).

---

## Output format

Combine all agent results into a single prioritised report:

```
## Code Quality Report
**Scope:** [files audited]
**Branch:** [current branch]
**Date:** [today]

### 🔴 Must fix before PR merge
[Issues that would fail review or cause runtime errors — one line per issue with file:line]

### 🟡 Should fix in this PR
[Issues that affect maintainability or violate conventions — one line per issue with file:line]

### 🔵 Backlog (log, don't block)
[Minor style issues, missing test cases for edge cases — one line per issue]

### ✅ No issues found
[List checks that passed cleanly]

### Summary
X must-fix · Y should-fix · Z backlog items
```

Do not suggest refactors beyond the scope of the changed files.
Do not modify any files — report only.

---
name: contentful-register-component
description: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
allowed-tools: Read, Edit, Bash
---

# Contentful Component Registration

Studio Experiences definitions are now **generated from code** — you never write a
`defineComponents` entry by hand. The source of truth is the component's `Props` type,
annotated with `@cf` JSDoc tags.

## Steps

### 1. Move the component into `experiences/`

The codegen only processes files under
`overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/`. If the component isn't there yet,
move it (or create it) in that folder.

### 2. Add `/** @cf-register */` to the component

Place it immediately before the component's `const` declaration:

```tsx
/** @cf-register */
const MyComponent = ({ ... }: MyComponentProps) => { ... };

export default MyComponent;
```

### 3. Annotate every prop in the `Props` type

Props without a `@cf` tag are silently skipped — omitting the tag is how you exclude a prop from the Contentful definition.

```tsx
type MyComponentProps = {
  /** @cf Headline */
  headline: string;

  /** @cf Body Copy, longText */
  body?: string;

  /** @cf Hero Image, media */
  heroImage?: string;

  /** @cf Layout, select */
  layout?: 'left' | 'right';

  internalId?: string;
};
```

**Tag syntax:**

| Tag | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `/** @cf Display Name */` | Infer control from the TS type (see table below) |
| `/** @cf Display Name, control */` | Override the inferred control |

Props without any `@cf` tag are silently skipped — no tag needed to exclude a prop.

**Type → control inference table:**

| TypeScript type | Inferred control | Contentful variable type |
|----------------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| `string` | `shortText` | Text |
| `boolean` | `toggle` | Boolean |
| `number` | `number` | Number |
| string literal union (`'a' \| 'b'`) | `select` | Text |

**Valid explicit controls:** `shortText`, `longText`, `select`, `toggle`, `number`, `media`

**Auto-skipped:** props starting with `on` (event handlers), `children` (emits
`children: true` on the component registration instead), and any prop with no `@cf` tag.

### 4. Run the generator

```bash
npm run generate:contentful
```

This rewrites `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`
automatically. Verify the output looks correct, then commit both the annotated
component and the updated `definitions.ts`.

### 5. Verify

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit
npm run generate:contentful:check
```

`--check` exits zero if `definitions.ts` is in sync with the source files.

---

## Notes

- **Never edit `definitions.ts` by hand** — it is autogenerated and will be overwritten
  on the next run.
- The pre-commit hook auto-runs the generator whenever an `experiences/*.tsx` file is
  staged, so `definitions.ts` stays in sync automatically.
- `children: ReactNode` → use `children: true` convention; the generator handles this
  automatically when it sees a `children` prop.
- `thumbnailUrl` is left blank until a real Contentful account exists.
- Component `id` is auto-derived as kebab-case of the filename
  (`myComponent.tsx` → `my-component`).
- Component `name` is auto-derived as Title Case of the id words
  (`my-component` → `My Component`).

2	name: new-component
3	description: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
4	---
5	
6	Scaffold a new Zimmermann custom component.
7	
8	The component name is: $ARGUMENTS
9	
10	## Conventions
11	
12	Follow [.claude/rules/conventions.md](../../rules/conventions.md) (naming, folder layout,
13	cross-cutting rules), [components.md](../../rules/components.md) (props types, JSDoc policy,
14	composition, Storybook categorisation), and [css.md](../../rules/css.md) (Chakra token usage)
15	— together the single source of truth for scaffolding. Higher-level project rules live in
16	[AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md). Do not restate rules here — read those files before
17	scaffolding.
18	
19	Key implications for scaffolding:
20	- Component lives in its own folder: `componentName/index.tsx` (Zimmermann-authored) or
21	  `component-name/index.tsx` (override of a base SF component).
22	- Props type named `<ComponentName>Props`, declared at the top of `index.tsx` by default.
23	- Storybook story is mandatory; Vitest only when the component owns non-trivial logic.
24	
25	## Steps
26	
27	1. Read one nearby existing custom component under [overrides/app/components/](../../../overrides/app/components/) to match code style, import order, and Chakra usage. If no Zimmermann-authored component exists yet, read a base template component from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/` and convert the style to TypeScript + Chakra props.
28	
29	2. Create `overrides/app/components/<componentName>/index.tsx`:
30	   - Functional React component, named export (`export function <ComponentName>`) plus default export.
31	   - `type <ComponentName>Props = { ... }` at the top of the file.
32	   - JSDoc above the component if it will be consumed by ≥2 callers (shared/Tier 2).
33	   - Chakra primitives for layout (`Box`, `Flex`, `Text`, etc.) using theme tokens — no hardcoded hex, pixel spacing, or raw font sizes.
34	   - No data-fetching hooks of any kind (commerce SDK hooks like `useCurrentBasket`/`useCurrentCustomer`/`useProduct`, or React Query) — accept data as props; the parent (a page or container component) owns data fetching. See components.md → Composition → Container/presentational separation. Exception: Context-backed, app-wide static-content hooks (`useIntl`, `useUiCopy`) may be called directly — they read from a Provider mounted once at the app root and degrade gracefully with none present, so they don't create the reuse problem this rule exists to prevent. See components.md's exception note for the full reasoning.
35	
36	3. Create `overrides/app/components/<componentName>/index.stories.tsx` — but first decide
37	   if a story is needed at all. Per [components.md](../../rules/components.md) →
38	   **Storybook**, purely internal sub-components that only render inside one parent
39	   don't need their own story; cover their variants via the parent. If a story *is* needed:
40	   - Storybook 8.6 CSF3 default export.
41	   - Pick the right category prefix from components.md — `Foundation/`, `Elements/`,
42	     `Layout/`, `Commerce/`, `Forms/`, `Pages/`, or `Contentful/`. Ask the developer if it's
43	     not obvious which one fits (with your recommendation).
44	   - `title: '<Category>/<ComponentName>'` (e.g. `'Commerce/ProductTile'`,
45	     `'Layout/Header'`).
46	   - At least one named export `Default`. Add named exports for meaningful states only —
47	     not every prop combination.
48	   - Add a `play` function only if the component has interactive behaviour worth asserting.
49	
50	4. If the component owns non-trivial logic (branching, prop→JSX mapping decisions, event wiring), create `index.test.ts`/`index.test.tsx` (Vitest) in the same folder — even if that logic's effects are also covered by a hook's own test or a parent's assembly-level Storybook `play`. Resolve any duplication by mocking the hook/child whose internals are proven elsewhere and testing only this component's own contract, not by skipping the file. See testing.md's note under "What to test (and what to skip)". Skip only when the component has no branching/decision logic at all (pure prop interpolation).
51	
52	5. Optional: if the props type exceeds ~30 lines or will be consumed by sibling files, move it to `types.ts` in the same folder. Otherwise leave it inline.
53	
54	6. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and confirm zero new errors.
55	
56	## Constraints
57	
58	- Do not modify any existing files (no auto-wiring into routes, parents, or the theme registry).
59	- Do not add npm packages — see [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) Hard Rule 7.
60	- Do not import from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` source directly — re-export from `@salesforce/retail-react-app/...` paths.
61	- For new icons, use `@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/icons`; if a needed icon is missing, ask the developer.
62	
63	## Output
64	
65	Tell the developer:
66	- The paths of every file created.
67	- The import to copy: `import <ComponentName> from '.../components/<componentName>'` (no filename — resolves via `index.tsx`).
68	- A one-sentence note on where it likely wires in, or ask if unsure.
69	- A reminder that `npx tsc --noEmit` was run and passed.
70

Scaffold a new Zimmermann custom component.

The component name is: $ARGUMENTS

## Conventions

Follow [.claude/rules/conventions.md](../../rules/conventions.md) (naming, folder layout,
cross-cutting rules), [components.md](../../rules/components.md) (props types, JSDoc policy,
composition, Storybook categorisation), and [css.md](../../rules/css.md) (Chakra token usage)
— together the single source of truth for scaffolding. Higher-level project rules live in
[AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md). Do not restate rules here — read those files before
scaffolding.

Key implications for scaffolding:
- Component lives in its own folder: `componentName/index.tsx` (Zimmermann-authored) or
  `component-name/index.tsx` (override of a base SF component).
- Props type named `<ComponentName>Props`, declared at the top of `index.tsx` by default.
- Storybook story is mandatory; Vitest only when the component owns non-trivial logic.

## Steps

1. Read one nearby existing custom component under [overrides/app/components/](../../../overrides/app/components/) to match code style, import order, and Chakra usage. If no Zimmermann-authored component exists yet, read a base template component from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/` and convert the style to TypeScript + Chakra props.

2. Create `overrides/app/components/<componentName>/index.tsx`:
   - Functional React component, named export (`export function <ComponentName>`) plus default export.
   - `type <ComponentName>Props = { ... }` at the top of the file.
   - JSDoc above the component if it will be consumed by ≥2 callers (shared/Tier 2).
   - Chakra primitives for layout (`Box`, `Flex`, `Text`, etc.) using theme tokens — no hardcoded hex, pixel spacing, or raw font sizes.
   - No data-fetching hooks of any kind (commerce SDK hooks like `useCurrentBasket`/`useCurrentCustomer`/`useProduct`, or React Query) — accept data as props; the parent (a page or container component) owns data fetching. See components.md → Composition → Container/presentational separation. Exception: Context-backed, app-wide static-content hooks (`useIntl`, `useUiCopy`) may be called directly — they read from a Provider mounted once at the app root and degrade gracefully with none present, so they don't create the reuse problem this rule exists to prevent. See components.md's exception note for the full reasoning.

3. Create `overrides/app/components/<componentName>/index.stories.tsx` — but first decide
   if a story is needed at all. Per [components.md](../../rules/components.md) →
   **Storybook**, purely internal sub-components that only render inside one parent
   don't need their own story; cover their variants via the parent. If a story *is* needed:
   - Storybook 8.6 CSF3 default export.
   - Pick the right category prefix from components.md — `Foundation/`, `Elements/`,
     `Layout/`, `Commerce/`, `Forms/`, `Pages/`, or `Contentful/`. Ask the developer if it's
     not obvious which one fits (with your recommendation).
   - `title: '<Category>/<ComponentName>'` (e.g. `'Commerce/ProductTile'`,
     `'Layout/Header'`).
   - At least one named export `Default`. Add named exports for meaningful states only —
     not every prop combination.
   - Add a `play` function only if the component has interactive behaviour worth asserting.

4. If the component owns non-trivial logic (branching, prop→JSX mapping decisions, event wiring), create `index.test.ts`/`index.test.tsx` (Vitest) in the same folder — even if that logic's effects are also covered by a hook's own test or a parent's assembly-level Storybook `play`. Resolve any duplication by mocking the hook/child whose internals are proven elsewhere and testing only this component's own contract, not by skipping the file. See testing.md's note under "What to test (and what to skip)". Skip only when the component has no branching/decision logic at all (pure prop interpolation).

5. Optional: if the props type exceeds ~30 lines or will be consumed by sibling files, move it to `types.ts` in the same folder. Otherwise leave it inline.

6. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and confirm zero new errors.

## Constraints

- Do not modify any existing files (no auto-wiring into routes, parents, or the theme registry).
- Do not add npm packages — see [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) Hard Rule 7.
- Do not import from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` source directly — re-export from `@salesforce/retail-react-app/...` paths.
- For new icons, use `@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/icons`; if a needed icon is missing, ask the developer.

## Output

Tell the developer:
- The paths of every file created.
- The import to copy: `import <ComponentName> from '.../components/<componentName>'` (no filename — resolves via `index.tsx`).
- A one-sentence note on where it likely wires in, or ask if unsure.
- A reminder that `npx tsc --noEmit` was run and passed.

1	---
2	name: onboarding
3	description: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
4	---
5	
6	Welcome the developer or QA engineer and explain what this skill does in one sentence.
7	Then proceed through the phases below. Ask one question at a time. Do not front-load.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Phase 1 — Role and context
12	
13	Ask:
14	> "Are you joining as a developer or a QA engineer?"
15	
16	Wait for the answer. Then:
17	
18	**If developer:** Ask:
19	> "Which squad are you on — Squad A (checkout, cart, payments, order management, tax, GivX) or Squad B (Homepage, PDP, PLP, search, account, Brochureware Content)?"
20	
21	**If QA:** No squad question needed — QA covers both squads.
22	
23	Ask (both roles):
24	> "Is this your first time working on this project, or are you returning on a new machine?"
25	
26	New = full walkthrough. Returning on new machine = focus on mechanical setup, skip orientation.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Phase 2 — Mechanical setup checks
31	
32	Run these checks inline using the Bash tool. Report results as you go.
33	
34	```bash
35	node --version
36	npm --version
37	claude --version 2>/dev/null || echo "NOT FOUND"
38	command -v coderabbit &>/dev/null && { coderabbit --version; coderabbit auth status; } || echo "NOT FOUND (required)"
39	git branch --show-current
40	ls -la .git/hooks/ | grep -E 'pre-commit|commit-msg' || echo "hooks missing"
41	[ -f .env.shared ] || echo ".env.shared missing"
42	for t in dev test sit uat staging prod; do
43	  [ -f ".env.$t" ] || echo ".env.$t missing"
44	done
45	[ -f .env ] || echo ".env missing"
46	```
47	
48	For each issue found:
49	
50	**Hooks missing:**
51	> "The git hooks aren't installed on this machine. Run both of these now:"
52	```bash
53	cp scripts/hooks/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
54	cp scripts/hooks/commit-msg .git/hooks/commit-msg && chmod +x .git/hooks/commit-msg
55	```
56	Verify after: `ls -la .git/hooks/ | grep -E 'pre-commit|commit-msg'`
57	
58	**On develop or main:**
59	> "You're on the `{branch}` branch. You must always work on a feature branch. Create one now:"
60	```bash
61	git checkout -b feature/your-ticket-onboarding-setup
62	```
63	
64	**Not fully initialized yet** (`.env.shared` missing, or any `.env.<tier>` file missing):
65	> "Environment config isn't fully set up on this machine yet. Run:"
66	```bash
67	npm run env -- init
68	```
69	> "This scaffolds `.env.shared` (values shared across every tier) and one `.env.<tier>` file per
70	> deployment tier (dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod), pulls in whatever's already been published to
71	> this repo's GitHub Environments (Settings > Environments), and auto-fetches your Contentful
72	> Delivery/Preview tokens once you've filled in a personal `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN`.
73	> Fill in any values it reports as still blank — `npm run env -- validate` shows what's missing —
74	> then activate a tier with `npm run env -- dev` (or whichever tier you're working against).
75	> Full command reference is in `.env.sample`'s header comment."
76	> `init` skips any file that already exists and only scaffolds what's missing, so it's always
